source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf models are poor forecasters. 14 models tested zero-shot and with scratchpad prompts on questions after their cutoff.
numbers: Random baseline Brier .250; human crowd .149; best baseline GPT-4-1106-Preview .208; most models near or worse than .25.
limits: Brier SEs assume iid questions; time-series data so SE too small. Crowd forecasts come from 5 platforms.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting of a model gives almost no forecasting skill. A scaffold must add something beyond a good prompt.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Full system: news retrieval, scratchpad reasoning, fine-tuning on self-generated reasonings that beat the crowd, ensembling. Approaches crowd; beats it on selected questions.
numbers: Test Brier .179 vs crowd .149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. When crowd is uncertain (.3-.7): .199 vs .246. Average of system and crowd (crowd weight 4x) .146 vs .149. Fine-tuning set 13,253 samples.
limits: System worse when crowd is very certain: it hedges (safety training), rarely outputs low probabilities. Worse on later retrieval dates.
agent_relevance: Rarely gives extreme probabilities. An agent needs a check that lets it commit when evidence is strong.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ablations show retrieval and fine-tuning carry the gain, the reasoning prompt carries little.
numbers: No fine-tuning: .186 (+.007). No fine-tuning and no retrieval: .206, same as best baseline .208. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4: .182. Newer GPT-4-1106 beats GPT-4-0613 by .02.
limits: One system, one test period.
agent_relevance: Evidence retrieval matters more than prompt tricks. The prompt already says think like a superforecaster and consider the base rate, yet the separate effect is only minor.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Model-side analog of training: fine-tune on the model's own reasonings whose forecasts beat the crowd. Filter: drop pairs more than 0.15 from crowd, average target with crowd to avoid overconfidence.
numbers: Selected from 16 candidate forecasts per question (4 scratchpad prompts, 2 models).
limits: Needs crowd forecasts for training questions.
agent_relevance: Learn which reasoning leads to good Brier, not a fixed rule list.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Median of 12 LLMs matches a human crowd of 925 forecasters on 31 binary Metaculus questions (equivalence test, wide bounds).
numbers: LLM crowd Brier .20 (SD .12) vs human crowd .19 (SD .19), t(60)=.19, p=.85. Equivalence bound Cohen d=.5 = .081 Brier. Single models: GPT-4 .15, GPT-4+Bing .16, Bard .19, Claude 2 .21, Llama-2-70B .25, Coral .38.
limits: Only 31 questions; wide equivalence bounds; individual models mostly worse than humans. Acquiescence bias: mean predictions significantly above 50% though outcomes about evenly split.
agent_relevance: Aggregating several samples or models is a cheap debiasing step. Audit the agent for a yes-bias.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Showing the human median to GPT-4 and Claude 2 improves them. Models move in proportion to distance from the human number.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier .17 to .14 (p=.003); Claude 2 .22 to .15 (p<.001). Interval width GPT-4 17.75 to 14.22; Claude 2 11.67 to 8.28. Update size vs initial gap: r=.88 (GPT-4), r=.87 (Claude 2). N=186 forecast pairs per model.
limits: Same 31 questions; human median is strong information; this is not training.
agent_relevance: Models update in the right direction when given an outside-view number. Supports a state that supplies a base rate.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Humans with an LLM advisor forecast more accurately, even an advisor told to be overconfident and ignore base rates. Preregistered randomized study.
numbers: N=991 analysed (1,152 recruited, Prolific), 6 questions. Accuracy gain 24-28% over control (weaker DaVinci-003 giving no predictions). Without one outlier item: superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy assistant +29%.
limits: Outlier driven; control model weaker and gave no numbers, so effect may be any-number-helps. No decline in crowd diversity found. Not a test of training.
agent_relevance: A numeric second opinion helps humans; bad advice is not much worse than good, so the gain may come from anchoring.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 1: 38 single-idea prompts on 100 ForecastBench questions, 4 models (Sonnet 3.5, Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B). Preregistered mixed model found no prompt that significantly helped.
numbers: Mixed-model estimates for best prompts: Frequency-Based Reasoning -.014, Base Rate First -.011, Chain of Thought -.011, Step-Back -.011 (all adj. p=.774). Secondary one-sample t-tests: Frequency-Based -.019 (N=370, adj p=.022), Base Rate First -.016 (N=390, adj p=.036), Step-Back -.015 (adj p=.036).
limits: Effects of about .01-.02 Brier. The evidence is the secondary, less robust analysis. About 3,600-3,800 forecasts per model.
agent_relevance: Human-training content such as start from the base rate gives a small gain in a model, not a large one. Do not count on a prompt-only training module.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Telling the model to reason as a Bayesian, or to propose-evaluate-select, made forecasts significantly worse.
numbers: Bayesian Reasoning +.030 Brier (z=5.44, p<.001, adj p<.001); Propose-Evaluate-Select +.033 (z=6.12, p<.001). These prompts made forecasts more decisive: mean distance from 0.5 of 17.2 to 19.9 points vs 11.9 to 13.4 for control, re-read and anti-anchoring prompts.
limits: Mechanism is likely overconfidence, not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: a human debiasing instruction (use Bayes) harmed the model. Test every training-style instruction before adding it. Fits SCHEMA section 4b not-to-add.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 2: compound prompts, automatic prompt generators, published academic prompts, plus o1 and o1-mini. Combining human-training prompts did not help.
numbers: Brier by model: o1-mini .217, o1 .216, Llama .218, GPT-4o .208, Sonnet .207. All Human prompt -.009, Base Rate First+Frequency -.004 (adj p .985). Only the superforecaster-authored Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt (from Karger 2024) was significantly worse.
limits: Same 100 questions; knowledge cutoffs before Dec 2024 resolutions.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models gain nothing from human-style forecasting prompts. Prompt stacks do not add up.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Dynamic benchmark. Superforecasters beat the public and the best LLM, and the gap is larger on combination questions.
numbers: Overall Brier: superforecasters .096, public .121 (p<.001), best LLM on 200-item subset Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122. On combination questions: superforecasters .076, public .096, GPT-4o .130; gap .054 vs GPT-4o is larger than the .026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4. Best LLMs had crowd freeze values for market questions.
limits: LLM prompts included crowd values. Question mix is dataset questions plus market questions.
agent_relevance: The gap to practiced humans remains large in this test; the agent should not claim parity.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: On 464 Metaculus questions, o3 beats the crowd benchmark from earlier work but stays far behind expert forecasters.
numbers: o3 median-ensemble Brier .1352 (SE .0097); o3-pro .1386; GPT-4.1 .1542; o4-mini .1589; DeepSeek-v3 .1798; GPT-4o .1883; GPT-4o-mini .2743. Experts .023 on their subset versus o3 .135 (paper text). Models overconfident on likely events; fine below 10%.
limits: Author notes Brier is not comparable across question sets; expert sets are small (some categories under 20 questions). Paper first called experts superforecasters (a trademark).
agent_relevance: Calibration plots show high-probability overconfidence, so a rule capping confidence on likely events is worth testing.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future
finding: RL on resolved prediction-market questions with Brier reward trains a 14B model to match o1 and calibrate better. This is training by outcomes, the machine analog of practice with feedback.
numbers: 1,265 hold-out questions. DeepSeek-R1 14B Brier .215, ECE .089; ReMax ensemble-7 .190, ECE .062; Modified-GRPO .192, ECE .054; o1 .202, ECE .093; Polymarket .151, ECE .043. Simulated Polymarket trading: $52 vs $39 for o1.
limits: Still .039 Brier behind the market (p<.001). Needs 10k to 100k resolved questions. Noisy delayed rewards.
agent_relevance: Human training lasts under an hour; the machine version needs 100,000 questions. Our scaffold has no gradient step, so any module must act at inference time.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Schoenegger (2025) LLMs Can Teach Themselves to Better Predict the Future
finding: Self-play DPO: rank pairs of the model's own reasonings by distance to the real outcome and fine-tune. No human reasoning samples.
numbers: Phi-4 14B Brier .221 base, .214 randomized-label control, .200 tuned (95% CI .191-.209). DeepSeek-R1 14B .197 after tuning. Ignorance benchmark .25.
limits: Randomized-label control already improves a little, so part of the gain is format or exposure. 14B models only.
agent_relevance: Feedback on Brier shaped reasoning without hand-written rules. Closest AI analog to tournament feedback.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical consistency (negation, paraphrase, conditional, arbitrage) of LLM forecasts correlates with their later Brier score. A patching forecaster fixes checks it trained on but not held-out ones and does not improve accuracy.
numbers: Arbitrage-profit metric and a frequentist metric; 10 check types; 3,000-question long-horizon consistency benchmark resolving 2028.
limits: Abstract and intro opened; per-model correlations not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Consistency checks are an instant, code-checkable test (the probability sum rule is the first CHAMPS-style rule). Training to fix them does not generalize, so use them as a check, not a target.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: ReAct agent with search and a Python tool for simulation matches the crowd; the same base LM without tools is much worse.
numbers: RTF median of 3 Brier .169, accuracy 72.4%; mean of 3 .170, 73.9%; crowd .172, 73.8%; Halawi GPT-4o .177; base LM mean .218, median .228. Ensembling helps the agent (.169 vs .180 single) but not the base LM.
limits: Own question set; faces the leakage issues in the Pitfalls paper.
agent_relevance: A method inside an agent loop: tool use plus numeric simulation for the outside view. Effect about .05 Brier.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Claims that LLM forecasters match humans are weakened by leakage and by piggybacking on human forecasts that sit in training data or retrieval.
numbers: Two classes: temporal leakage (retrieval date filters leak, retrieval model trained on future data, cutoffs are not guarantees) and extrapolation problems.
limits: Argument paper, no new effect size.
agent_relevance: Treat every LLM-matches-crowd number above with caution, including Halawi and Lu.

source: FutureSearch (2025) Bench to the Future: A Pastcasting Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
finding: Pastcasting with a frozen offline corpus gives results comparable to live forecasts; single LLM forecasts are very noisy.
numbers: Hundreds of questions, tens of thousands of pages each. Some questions gave under 20% on one run and over 80% on another. No human baseline available.
limits: Authors state no human baseline yet.
agent_relevance: Run each question several times and take the median; one sample is not a forecast.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly: accuracy plateaus after the first interaction. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's choices (Bayesian teaching) keeps improving over rounds and generalizes to new tasks.
numbers: Flight-recommendation task, 5 rounds; simulated-user accuracy approaches 80% for the Bayesian assistant. Bayesian teaching beats oracle teaching. Medium LLMs after tuning beat stronger models and human participants.
limits: Teaching is by fine-tuning on a synthetic task, not by prompting. Human users' inconsistent choices cap accuracy.
agent_relevance: Contrast with the prompt study: telling a model to be Bayesian hurts, but training on Bayesian examples works. Training needs examples, not instructions.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: CHAMPS KNOW training
finding: Human anchor for the module. Under 1 hour of training (CHAMPS KNOW) improved Brier scores 6 to 11% across four tournament years.
numbers: Year 1: probability-trained n=119 standardized Brier -.05, scenario-trained n=113 -.06, control n=152 +.07; improvements 10% and 11%. Year 2: trained vs control n=194, 12% improvement, t(395)=5.95, p<.001. Year 3: 6%. Year 4: 7% (t(225)=2.20, p=.028).
limits: Volunteers (83% male, mean 41 years). Which prong helped is not isolated.
agent_relevance: What a model-side module should aim to copy: small, cheap, content on base rates and comparison classes. Human gain 6-11%; prompt gain in models is under about 10% of Brier at best.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: CHAMPS KNOW training
finding: Explanations showed which parts of training mattered: 69% of trained forecasters' explanations invoked a principle; use of comparison classes correlated with lower Brier. Practice and cognitive ability contributed largely independently.
numbers: 6,714 explanations from trained forecasters (76% submitted). Mediation: training effect partly runs through more forecasts per question.
limits: Correlational inside the trained group. The 'lasted a year' claim was not found in this paper; effects are measured within each year.
agent_relevance: Check an agent's rationale for a named reference class before trusting its probability.

source: Moore et al. (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition (Management Science)
finding: Not opened this session (publisher returned 403). Listed in SUBFIELDS.md as key work; cited only as a pointer.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Do not use as evidence until read.
agent_relevance: Fetch the author PDF in a later pass.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Prompt used in the system asks the model to be a superforecaster, aggregate considerations, and check whether it is too confident or not confident enough, including the base rate.
numbers: Prompt chosen from a sweep on the validation set; reasoning prompt alone gives a minor gain (.206 vs .208 baseline once retrieval and fine-tuning are removed).
limits: Prompt wording tuned to one model and period.
agent_relevance: A self-check step 'am I too confident, what is the base rate' has been used in a working forecaster, but its separate value is small.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Top LLMs scored best when given the crowd's current value (freeze values) on market questions; without it they did worse.
numbers: Superforecasters .096 vs top model .122 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) on 200-item subset; best models had freeze values.
limits: Exact no-crowd score not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Supplying an outside-view anchor lifts the model more than any instruction. Matches the silicon-crowd result.
